extracted.intended_audience: administrative law practitioners, federal agencies, agency adjudicators/administrators, and courts (litigants challenging agency rulemaking and NEPA compliance)
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and tests for judicial review of federal agency rulemaking and licensing proceedings, especially under the Administrative Procedure Act (5 U.S.C. § 553) and NEPA; includes when courts may require additional procedures, and threshold rules for intervenors raising novel issues (e.g., energy conservation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory minima under 5 U.S.C. § 553
rubrics_metrics.description: 5 U.S.C. § 553 establishes the maximum procedural requirements that Congress was willing to have the courts impose upon federal agencies in conducting rulemaking proceedings; agencies are free to grant additional procedural rights in the exercise of their discretion, but reviewing courts are generally not free to impose them if the agencies have not chosen to grant them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies may provide more procedural protections but courts should not engraft their own procedural preferences onto agencies. Only in extremely rare circumstances should courts require procedures beyond the statutory minima.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency discretion to formulate procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: Formulation of procedures should basically be left within the discretion of the agencies to which Congress has confided substantive judgments; agencies are familiar with the industries they regulate and better positioned than courts to design procedural rules adapted to the peculiarities of the industry and tasks of the agency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts should defer to agency choices about scope of inquiry, sequencing of hearings, intervention rules, and similar procedural matters unless constitutional constraints or extremely compelling circumstances exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quasi-judicial exception (due process for few exceptionally affected)
rubrics_metrics.description: When an agency in a rulemaking is making a 'quasi-judicial' determination affecting a very small number of persons 'exceptionally affected, in each case upon individual grounds,' additional procedures may be required to afford due process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a narrow exception; courts should determine whether the particular rulemaking has an adjudicatory character that justifies extra procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial limitation on prescribing procedures on remand
rubrics_metrics.description: If a court finds additional evidence is necessary for adequate review, the court may remand to the agency but generally may not dictate the methods, procedures, and time dimension of the needed inquiry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts should avoid 'propel[ling] the court into the domain which Congress has set aside exclusively for the administrative agency' (Chenery principle). The agency should decide how to develop evidence and modify prior decisions in light of new evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grounds for extraordinary judicial intervention
rubrics_metrics.description: There may be circumstances (e.g., constitutional constraints or extremely compelling circumstances, or a totally unjustified departure from well-settled agency procedures of long standing) that could justify courts imposing additional procedures, but such circumstances are extremely rare.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Absent those rare circumstances, courts should not impose extra procedural devices simply because they believe different procedures would be 'best' or more sensitive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court's role in reviewing adequacy of record vs procedural form
rubrics_metrics.description: A reviewing court should engage in APA-style review to determine whether the challenged rule finds sufficient justification in the administrative proceedings (e.g., arbitrary and capricious review), but should not stray beyond the judicial province to explore or impose the agency's preferred procedural format.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the record is inadequate to support the rule, the court can remand for further factual development but should not prescribe how the agency must conduct that development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Threshold for intervenors asserting novel issues (energy conservation)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission required intervenors to present only energy conservation alternatives that were 'reasonably available,' would in their aggregate effect curtail demand for electricity to a level at which the proposed facility would not be needed, and were susceptible of a reasonable degree of proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intervenors must meet this threshold before the agency must consider the issues; mere assertion without showing does not oblige reopening or detailed consideration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intervenor pleading and proof obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: Intervenors must state clear and reasonably specific contentions in a timely fashion, and have a burden of coming forward with some affirmative showing if they wish novel contentions (such as energy conservation) explored further.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to propose proper findings and to present affirmative evidence can lead boards to treat issues as not contested or to decline consideration; courts defer to agency procedures that require a minimum showing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Board 'threshold test' for requiring further inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board's stated procedure required a showing sufficient to require reasonable minds to inquire further — a threshold test within the agency's discretion to screen issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This 'threshold' approach is a permissible procedure for agencies to manage limited adjudicatory resources and to prevent frivolous or unsupported contentions from expanding proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement of offer of proof to justify expanded procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission emphasized that proponents of expanded procedures (e.g., cross-examination or discovery) must make an offer of proof or otherwise suggest what substantive matters they would develop under different procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Absent an offer of proof showing what additional evidence would be produced, denial of cross-examination or discovery in rulemaking does not necessarily deny meaningful opportunity to participate.

rubrics_metrics.name: NEPA scope principles (adverse effects and irreversible commitments)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under NEPA, agencies must consider adverse environmental effects which cannot be avoided and irreversible and irretrievable commitments of resources when implementing projects (references to 42 U.S.C. §§ 4332(2)(C)(ii), (v)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This principle supports consideration of long-lived nuclear waste impacts and other environmental consequences in environmental impact statements and agency licensing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on judicial intrusion into administrative processes (e.g., advisory committee elaboration)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is an unjustifiable intrusion for a court to require an agency to return an advisory committee report (ACRS) to that committee for further elaboration; the court lacked statutory justification for such micromanagement of agency procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts should avoid directing agencies how to use or clarify advisory reports; agencies retain discretion to manage internal/expert advisory processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency compliance verification by courts
rubrics_metrics.description: The court must determine whether the agency complied with the procedures mandated by relevant statutes; if the agency complied with statutory requirements, courts should not find procedural inadequacy simply because they would have preferred other procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: where agency actions appear to satisfy § 553, courts should not overturn rules merely because different procedural devices might have been employed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Considerations for retroactive application of new rules
rubrics_metrics.description: In deciding whether to apply a new rule retroactively, agencies should weigh factors such as departure from prior practice, degree of reliance on past practice, and burdens imposed by retroactive application; the Commission may choose not to apply a new rule retroactively to cases progressed to final order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Retroactivity is a discretionary agency judgment informed by fairness and reliance concerns; courts will consider those factors in review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of court scrutiny of opportunity to participate
rubrics_metrics.description: A court may 'scrutinize the record as a whole to insure that genuine opportunities to participate in a meaningful way were provided,' but this scrutiny should not be used to prescribe the particular procedural format the agency must follow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court review focuses on whether participants in fact had meaningful opportunity, not on whether the court would have structured the process differently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency latitude in novel, evolving subject-matter areas
rubrics_metrics.description: In emergent or evolving areas (e.g., early-stage energy conservation techniques), agencies and intervenors have responsibilities: agencies must develop an adequate record when appropriate, and intervenors must present clear, specific, timely contentions with affirmative supporting evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Given novelty, agencies may adopt workable procedural rules that balance development of the record with practicality; courts should respect that balancing.
